At the market: how much is it?
You count to 100, ask how much something costs, tell the time and name the days of the week.
abbreviated: kg; in speech: un kil
How much is a kilo of tomatoes?
I would like ten eggs, please.
On Saturdays I go to the market.
To use “de” after numbers from 20 upwards (douăzeci de lei).
To ask how much something costs and understand prices in lei and bani.
To ask politely for what you want: “Vreau…”, “Aș vrea…”.
To tell the time: “e ora trei”, “trei și un sfert”, “patru fără zece”.
To know the days of the week and the parts of the day.
On Saturday morning, Mrs Pop takes Nora to the Mărăști market, the biggest market in Cluj. They stop at the stall of a farmer from the village of Florești, Mr Gheorghe.
Good morning, Mr Gheorghe! What lovely tomatoes you have today!
Good morning to you, teacher! They’re from my garden in Florești.
Good morning! How much is a kilo of tomatoes, please?
Nine lei a kilo. But for you, eight lei.
Then I’d like two kilos. And do you have eggs too?
Of course. Free-range eggs, one leu fifty each. How many would you like?
Ten, please. And a little cottage cheese.
The cheese is twenty-five lei a kilo. Half a kilo?
Yes, perfect. How much is it altogether?
Sixteen for the tomatoes, fifteen for the eggs, twelve fifty for the cheese… Forty-three lei fifty.
And six fifty change. Thank you very much! See you next Saturday too!
Nora, it’s a quarter to ten. Come on, quickly, the warm bread runs out at ten!
to have: dumneavoastră aveți (you have, formal)
to want: “aș vrea” = I would like
bani (subunit of the leu; also: money in general)
to want: dumneavoastră vreți (you want, formal)
“brânză de vaci” = fresh cottage cheese made from cow’s milk
to do, to make; “cât face?” = how much is it altogether?
to run out, to end: se termină
Numbers 11–19 end in “-sprezece”, but in speech they are shortened: “unsprezece” sounds like “unșpe”, “doisprezece” like “doișpe”. Always write the long form, but recognise the short one.
“ou” is read as one syllable (like “o” in English “go”), while “ouă” has two: “o-uă”.
“ieftin” begins with a short gliding “i”: “yef-tin”, not “i-ef-tin”.
Watch the stress: “sâmbătă” is stressed on the first syllable and “duminică” on the second: SÂM-bă-tă, du-MI-ni-că.
As with 1 and 2, “doisprezece” and “douăzeci și doi” also have a feminine form: “douăsprezece fete” (twelve girls), “douăzeci și două de case” (twenty-two houses).
From 20 upwards, “de” appears between the number and the noun. If the number ends in 01–19 (for example 101, 115), the “de” disappears again.
This is a very common mistake among foreigners: “douăzeci lei” is wrong. Always say “douăzeci de lei”.
Romania’s currency is the leu (plural: lei). One leu has 100 bani. Prices are often said briefly, without “lei” and “bani”: “șase cincizeci” = 6.50 lei.
How much is it altogether? (total price)
One leu fifty each. (1.50 lei for one)
Careful with “bani”: it means both the subunit of the leu and money in general. “N-am bani” = I have no money at all.
“A vrea” (to want) is a very common irregular verb. At the market or in a shop, the most polite form is “aș vrea” (the conditional, which you will learn later).
I would like a coffee, please. (polite)
Quantities are linked with “de”: “un kilogram de roșii” (a kilo of tomatoes), “o sticlă de apă” (a bottle of water), “jumătate de kil de brânză” (half a kilo of cheese).
For the time you use “ora” + the number (in the feminine!). Minutes are added with “și” or subtracted with “fără”.
What time is it? – It’s nine o’clock.
What time does it start? – At ten. (the time of an action: with “la”)
At stations, on the radio and in official schedules, time is given from 0 to 24: “ora paisprezece și treizeci” = 14:30.
Days are written with a small letter. The week starts on Monday.
I’m going to the market on Saturday. (this Saturday)
I go to the market on Saturdays. (every Saturday)

Parts of the day: dimineața (in the morning), la prânz (at lunchtime), după-amiaza (in the afternoon), seara (in the evening), noaptea (at night). “Dimineața beau cafea” = every morning I drink coffee.
What time is “patru fără un sfert”?
“fără un sfert” = 15 minutes before four o’clock.
How much is a kilo of apples?
I would like a loaf of bread, please.
A kilo of potatoes costs three lei.
It is a quarter past eight.
The cheese costs twenty-five lei a kilo.
I would like two kilos of tomatoes.
I, Mițu, have a very strict schedule. Listen!
On Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, at seven o’clock, Nora leaves for the office. Mrs Pop drinks coffee and reads the newspaper. I sleep in the armchair.
At one o’clock, Mrs Pop eats. I eat too, of course. Then I sleep again, until five.
On Saturdays, Mrs Pop and Nora go to the market. They come home with tomatoes, eggs and cheese. The cheese is for them, not for me. Unfair!
But today is Sunday. Sunday is my favourite day.
On Sundays Radu comes for lunch, at half past twelve. Ioana, his mother, comes too. Everybody sits at the table for two hours.
Today Mrs Pop is making sarmale. There are thirty-five sarmale in the pot. I count them.
Radu eats eight. Ioana eats five. Nora eats six and says: “They’re fantastic!” Mrs Pop eats only three, because she talks the whole time.
There are thirteen sarmale left. I look at the pot. The pot looks at me.
Mrs Pop laughs: “Mițu, no! Sarmale are not for tomcats!”
But Radu, under the table, gives me a little piece of meat. Radu is my favourite musician.
sarmale (cabbage leaves stuffed with meat, a traditional dish)
to give: el îmi dă (he gives me)

Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. Tap any word to see what it means. Four questions follow at the end.
My name is Gheorghe Moldovan and I am sixty-eight years old.
I’m from Florești, a village near Cluj. I have a big garden and four cows.
On Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays I sell vegetables at the Mărăști market.
I wake up at four in the morning. By six I’m already at the market.
My tomatoes cost eight or nine lei. They’re not cheap, but they’re very good.
Mrs Pop has been my customer for twenty years. She was my son’s teacher.
Now she has a tenant from Sweden. The girl speaks Romanian with an accent, but very nicely.
Mrs Pop was his son’s teacher.
